### [Let's start with basic assignment:]{.underline}

class(x)

```

print(y)
```

```{r}

y[2]
# negative means not: so i am slicing 2 to 4 out

```

#### Note:

Copying in R will do the reassignment but changes made in the copied variable doesn't change the original variable values

```{r}
# copying 
a <- 1:5
# let's assign a to b
b <- a
# Now let's change an element in b; a is not affected
b[1]<- 0
print(b)
print(a)
```

## [Vectorization:]{.underline}

A vector is a sequence of items of the same type: vector items can be coerced to the same type based on the order of coercion : character\>double\>integer\>logic. If you entered items of characters and doubles in a vector, the whole vector items are coerced into characters, if you have a vector of double and integers, it is coerced to double in that order. Vectorization is faster in operations than looping: Let's demonstration

```{r}
# example of vectors
g <- c("Joy","Steph","Mimmy")
h <- c(1,2,3,4,5)
l <- c(TRUE,FALSE,TRUE, FALSE)
#printing the vectors we have created: cat is used for outputing/printing
cat("g ---> ", g ,"\n")
cat("h ---> ", h ,"\n")
cat("l ---> ", l)
```

### **Order of Coercion of data types in a vector in R:**

```{r}
# Let's demonstrate the coercion in r: character takes precedence
s <- c(1,'Anyy',3)
print(s)
```

```{r}
# A few more example:
c(1, TRUE)        # numeric:    1  1    (TRUE becomes 1)
c(1L, 2.5)        # double:     1  2.5  (integer becomes double)
c(1, 2, "hello")  # character: "1" "2" "hello"
c(TRUE, FALSE, 1) # numeric:    1   0   1
```

```{r}
# let's loop through this :
results <- numeric(5) # create a variable to hold the loop results
for (x in 1:5){
  results[x] <- x^2
}
print(results)
```

```{r}
# we could have just used this vectorized operation: this is faster for large operations
results_1 <- (1:5)^2
print(results_1)

```

```{r}
# for the loopin we could have equally created a vector of unknown size
results3 <- c()
for (i in 1:5){
  results3[i] <- i^2
}
print(results3)
```

### Recycling Rule :

operating on vectors of different length, the shorter one is recycled into the longer one: The shorter vector should be a multiple of the longer one to allow normal computation if added it takes the first element in the short vector multiply it to the first item in the longer vector, takes the second element in the shorter vector multiply it to next element in the longer vector and repeats the process in the shorter vector for all elements in the longer vector

```{r}
a <- c(1,2,3,4)
b <- c(10,20)
a + b 
```

### Vector Arithmetic:

```{r}
scores <- c(2,3,4,1)
# addition
scores + 5  # adds 5 to every element results : 7,8,9,6
scores * 2  # multiplies by 2
scores / 2  # divides by 2
scores ^ 2  # squares 
scores - 5  # subtracts 5
scores > 3   # returns a logical value after comparing
```

### Useful vector functions:

```{r}
mean(scores)  # calculate mean of scores
max(scores)   # calculate maximum score
sum(scores)   # finds sum of scores
sort(scores)  # sort scores 
length(scores) # length of scores
```

### Indexing :

R indexing starts at 1 and not 0 as in python indexing

```{r}
scores[1]  # select first element
scores[1:3] # selects first to third element
scores[c(1,3)] # selects item 1 and 3
scores[scores>2] # filters or slices for scores greater than 2
```

## [**Matrices**]{.underline}

A matrix is a 2-dimensional vector all elements must be the same type. Matrices are essential for linear algebra and statistical computations. The dimnames is the dimension names. it is passed as a list of vectors.

NB: the byrow argument dictates how the matrix is filled. byrow = TRUE means you fill the matrix row wise. if byrow = FALSE, then it fills the matrix column by column

```{r}
# let's create some matrices : first argument is the data to form the matrix from
m <- matrix((1:6),ncol = 3,nrow = 2)
m
```

```{r}
# let's set the dimension names with the dimnames variable 
mx <- c(2,4,6,7,0,4,3,2)
m1 <- matrix(mx,nrow = 4, 
             ncol = 2,
             dimnames = list(c("R1","R2","R3","R4"),c("Col1","Col2"))
             )
m1
```

```{r}
# demonstration of fill byrow and colum
mx_row = matrix((1:6),nrow = 2, ncol = 3,
                byrow = TRUE,
                dimnames = list(c("R1","R2"),c("Col1","Col2","Col3"))
                )
mx_row
```

```{r}
# now let's do by column that is byrow = FASE
mx_col <- matrix((1:6),nrow = 2, ncol = 3,
                byrow = FALSE,
                dimnames = list(c("R1","R2"),c("Col1","Col2","Col3"))
                )
mx_col
```

### [Matrix Operation]{.underline}

```{r}
# matrix multiplication :
mby2 <-  matrix((1:3),nrow = 3, ncol = 1,
              dimnames = list(c("R1","R2","R3"),c("col1"))
              )
mby2
```

```{r}
# now let's do dome operations:In matrix mulitplication the number of columns in 
# in the first matrix must match the number of rows in the second matrix

mx_col %*% mby2
```

```{r}
# creating matrix mx_col
mx_col <- matrix(c(2,4,7,8,3,4,1,7,-2), ncol = 3, nrow = 3)
mx_col
```

```{r}
# determinant of matrix:
det(mx_col)

# transposition of matrix
t(mx_col)

# inverse of a matrix;
solve(mx_col)
```

### Slicing a matrix:

use the dimension to slice matrix[row,col]

```{r}
# selects all rows and column 1
mx_col[,1]

# select item at col 1: row 1
mx_col[1,1]
```

## [Flow control :]{.underline}

### Conditional statements

If statements works on only one value. if you have a vector of values and you use this type of if, statement, it only checks the first element in the vector and leaves the rest. use ifelse() to check conditions on vector of values.

```{r}
# let's demonstrate
score <- 85
# let's write an if statment to grade this results
if (score > 80) {grade <- "A"} else if (score >75) {
    grade < "B"} else {grade<- "C"}
grade
```

```{r}
# we could wrap the if statement in a function to use the return method
grader<- function(scores){
  if (scores>80){return("A")}
  else if(scores>75){return("B")}
  else {return("C")}
}
grader(score)
```

```{r}
# let's try it on a vector : it says the condition has length greater than 1
#scores <- c(50,75,83,60,45)
#if (scores > 80) {gdp <- "A"} else if (scores >75) {
#    gdp < "B"} else {gdp <- "C"}
#gdp
```

### ifelse()

```{r}
# let's see how ifelse() works on vectors: nested ifelse()
ifelse(
  (scores > 80),"A",ifelse((scores>75),"B", "C")
)
```

### Loops

##### For loops:

R has three looping constructs. Note that explicit loops are often unnecessary in R because most operations are vectorized.

```{r}
# Let's do few example:
for (i in 1:5){
  print(i)
}
```

```{r}
# let's update some totals while we loop: adds from 1 to 5
total <- 0
for (i in 1:5){
  total <- total + i
}
total
```

### **While loops :**

loops until a condition evaluates to False

```{r}
# Let's print until we get to 5: The loop automatically stop after 5
x = 0
while (x<=5){
  print(x)
  x<- x+1
}
```

Looping with break: use repeat

```{r}
# let's loop with break: let's print from zero to 3
n <- 0
repeat {
  print(n)
  n <- n+1
  if (n >= 4) break # break the loop when n = 4
}
```

```{r}
# let's collect items in a variable after looping 
res <- c()
for (name in c('James',"Nathaniel","Mic")){
  res<- c(res,name)
}
res
```

## [Writing Custom Functions]{.underline}

There different types of functions in R:

Named functions \~ standard functions, Anonymous functions,infix functions,recursive functions, higher order functions.

name_function \<- function(arg1, arg2...){

expression

return (value) }

```{r}
# let's look syntax of functions in R

add_two <- function(a,b){
  results <- a + b
  return (results)
}

# let's now execute our function that adds two numbers 
add_two(4,3)
```

```{r}
# let's write a function that calculate bmi and show us what to do
cal_bmi <- function (weight, height){
  height_m <-  height/100
  bmi <- weight/ height_m ^2
  if (bmi > 36) {print(paste(bmi,'Dude you are overweight: You need to be on diet'))}
  else if (bmi > 30) {print(paste(bmi,"You should start keeping an eye on your diet"))}
  else if ((20 < bmi)&(bmi <= 29)){print(paste(bmi,"That is great bmi; keep up with this life style"))}
  else {print(paste(bmi,"Undeer weight"))}
}
# let's try a bmi of 40 and a bmi of 18
cal_bmi(70,170)
cal_bmi(120,155)
```

**Functions with default arguments:**

The function comes with some default argument and when you don't change it it automatically runs

```{r}
greet_friend <- function(name, greeting = "Hello"){
  message <- paste(greeting,name)
  return(message)
}
greet_friend("Ella")
```

```{r}
# let' try and modify the greeting default value
greet_friend(name="Ella", greeting= "Chawchaw")
```

### Returning Multiple Values

R functions can only return a single object, but that object can be a list allowing you to return multiple values at once. We cam use a list to return multiple values

```{r}
# let's create a function that calculates, mean, sd , median,range and length
sta_summary <- function(x){
  summaries <- list(
    mean = mean(x),
    sd = sd(x),
    median = median(x),
    range = range(x),
    lenth = length(x)
  )
  return(summaries)
}
```

```{r}
# Now let's create a vector to text our function 
scor <- c(2:11)
describe <- sta_summary(scor)

# let's check some few summaries
describe$mean
describe$sd
describe$median
```

### Functions as Arguments (Higher-Order Functions)

In R, functions are first-class objects you can pass them as arguments to other functions. This is the foundation of the apply family.

```{r}
# let's write a function that takes the square function and a number
# we are going to square root the number twice

square_root_twice <- function(fun,x){
  results <- fun(fun(x))
  return (results)
}

square_root_twice(sqrt,16) # answer 2
```

#### lappy and sapply:

Both apply a function to every element of a list or vector the only difference is **what they return back**.

lapply returns a list and sapply tries as much to return a vector;

```{r}
# let's work some examples:
num <- (1:6)^2
l  <- lapply(num, sqrt)
s <- sapply(num,sqrt)
s
l
```

## [Scope and Environments]{.underline}

R uses lexical scoping a function looks for variables in the environment where it was defined, not where it is called. If a variable is outside the function creation environment or in the global environment we use the \<\<- arrow to tell R to look upper the levels of environments from the immediate environment up.

```{r}
# let's demonstrate 
x <- 10

# let's create a function that assigns a differnet value to x and see if it changes the gloabal x value of 10
no_change <- function(){
  x <- 100
  return(x)
}
# let's call the function and then x and see if the values are all changed to 100
no_change()
x
```

You see that global x \<- 10 was unchanged because a function picks it variables from the environment is it was created not where it was executed. Now let's create a function that can read the variable in a global environment or a level up above where it was declared:

```{r}
# let's create a counter variable and give it a value and update it from inside our function 
counter <- 0
increase_count <- function(){
  counter <<- counter +1
  return(counter)
}
# let's run an check what happens
increase_count()
counter
```

You see our function was able to look up above the creation environment to pic the variable counter. Even though counter was not created in the function environment. the \<\<- sign tells R to look up and find that counter variable

## [Error Handling in Functions]{.underline}

**What is Error Handling?**

Error handling means anticipating things that can go wrong in your function and dealing with them gracefully instead of letting your program crash.

R has three levels of problems

- `stop()` : throws an **error**, halts execution completely

- `warning()`: throws a **warning**, execution continues but flags something suspicious

- `message()`: prints an **informational message**, not an error at all

```{r}
# let's demonstrate this 
divide <- function(a,b){
  if (!is.numeric(a) | !is.numeric(b)){
    stop("Numbers must be numeric to divide")
  }
  if (b == 0){
    warning("Dividing by Zero returns infinity\n")
  }
  if (a<0){
    message("You are dividing by negative")
  }
  return(a/b)
}
```

```{r}
# let's try the first stop message : see how the function stops
#divide("a",2)
```

```{r}
# let's try the warning: 
divide(2,0)
```

```{r}
# let' induce a call of the message :
divide(-1,2)
```

#### Using try Catch code:

The tryCatch is used to handle errors, the function has an expression block and blocks to handle errors

and warnings and a final block to run regardless of whatever happens.

```{r}
# let's try to find square root
square_root<- function(x){
  result <- tryCatch(
    expr = {
      if (!is.numeric(x)) {stop("You need to enter a numeric value")}
      sqrt(x)
    },
    error = function(e){
      cat('This error occured\n',conditionMessage(e))
      return(NA)},
    warning = function(w){
      cat('You got this warning\n',conditionMessage(w))
      return(NA)},
    finally = {cat('\nWe attempted to run sqrt')}
  )
  return(result)
}
```

```{r}
square_root(-1)
```

```{r}
# let's run on a string and see if it immediately ends it
square_root("a")
```

## [Data Cleaning]{.underline}

In real life, data set are usually messy and needs to be cleaned for accurate data analysis. here are functions and tools for effective data cleaning workflow in R:

#### checking miss data

```{r}
# let's check miss data in the bikes data df2 : No missing data
sum(is.na(df2))
```

```{r}
# let's check the framingham dataset
framingham <- read.csv(
"D:/MACHINE_LEARNING/Framingham_project/framingham_heart_study.csv")
head(framingham,3)
```

```{r}
# let's check for missing values: total miss: 645 total missing data
sum(is.na(framingham))
```

```{r}
# checking missing by column: check for the sum of missing values in each column
count_na <- colSums(is.na(framingham))
data.frame(
  missing = count_na
)
```

```{r}
# let's load the full tidyverse for more work
library(tidyverse)
```

```{r}
# let's add more style: we calculate missing percent
na_counts <- colSums(is.na(framingham))
data.frame(
  column  = names(na_counts),
  missing = na_counts,
  percent = round(na_counts / nrow(framingham) * 100, 1)
) |> arrange(desc(missing))

```

#### Filling missing value

```{r}
# let's fill na in glucose and then later look at how to drop nas
framingham$glucose[is.na(framingham$glucose)] <- mean(framingham$glucose, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#let's again check the nas in glucose: worked
sum(is.na(framingham$glucose))
```

#### Removing all missing data

```{r}
# removes all nas and reassign it to the same dataframe
framingham <- na.omit(framingham)
```

```{r}
#let's check the dataframe again
na_count <- colSums(is.na(framingham))
data.frame(
  variables = names(na_count),
  missing = na_count,
  percent = round((na_count/ nrow(framingham)*100),1)
) %>% arrange(desc(missing))
```

#### Removing duplicates ;

Using disticnt : distinct automatically removes all duplicates

```{r}
framingham <- distinct(framingham)
```

#### Checking duplicates

```{r}
# there no duplicates in dataframe 2
df2[duplicated(df2),]
```
